obtained.how: university repository: Oregon State University's ScholarsArchive (the authors' institution) open PDF scan of FAO Fisheries Technical Paper No. 86 itself (303 PDF pages, text layer); Table 1 read on the page image

bibliography.checked_against: the title page (PDF pp. 1, 3) and the 'Preparation of this paper' page (PDF p. 4)
bibliography.note: Doudoroff, Peter & Shumway, Dean L. Dissolved oxygen requirements of freshwater fishes. FAO Fisheries Technical Paper No. 86 (FIRI/T86), FAO, Rome, June 1970; 291 p.; 'Distribution restricted'. Also Oregon Agricultural Experiment Station Special Report No. 281. (AGRIS lists it as 1971.) The parts relevant here were read in context (pp. 44, 55–56, 62, 71); the whole 291-page review was not read.

claims.claim: lethal at 0.5–1.6 mg/L in declining-oxygen tests (4-g fish; Burdick et al. 1954, via Doudoroff & Shumway 1970)
claims.source_value: loss of equilibrium, not death, is the endpoint: 4-g smallmouth in sealed vessels with declining O₂ at 11–27 °C lost equilibrium first at 0.9–1.6 mg/L, 50 % at 0.6–1.2 and 100 % at 0.5–1.0 mg/L; the median level rose by 40–62 % from the lowest to the highest temperature
claims.quote: Smallmouth bass 4 g 0.9-1.6 First* Declining O2 11-27 Burdick et al. (1954)
claims.conditions: Table 1, 'Summary of lethal levels of dissolved oxygen published after the year 1937'; the same table lists 255-g smallmouth at < 2.0 mg/L, 100 %, declining O₂, 15–25 °C (Black et al. 1954)
claims.note: D&S treat loss of equilibrium in sealed vessels as the 'lethal level' (p. 71: 'concentrations at which loss of equilibrium occurred in sealed vessels'); the paper should name the endpoint and the temperature span, since the levels rise with temperature

claims.claim: smallmouth in declining-oxygen tests died at 0.5–1.6 mg/L (Burdick et al. 1954, via Doudoroff & Shumway 1970)
claims.source_value: lost equilibrium (first fish to all fish) at 0.9–1.6 to 0.5–1.0 mg/L; 4-g fish, sealed vessels, 11–27 °C
claims.quote: concentrations at which loss of equilibrium occurred in sealed vessels
claims.note: suggested: 'smallmouth (4 g) in sealed, declining-oxygen tests lost equilibrium at 0.5–1.6 mg/L between 11 and 27 °C'

claims.claim: the lethal O₂ found in natural winterkills under the ice (Cooper & Washburn 1946) was accepted by Doudoroff & Shumway 1970 over caged-fish values
claims.quote: we cannot accept as valid Moore's conclusions concerning O2 concentrations
claims.conditions: Moore (1942) held fish in cages in lakes (winter lethal levels 2.3 mg/L for largemouth and pike, 1.5 for perch); D&S set against them Cooper & Washburn's natural under-ice thresholds (about 0.6 mg/L for largemouth, 0.4–0.3 for pike and yellow perch) and cite them 'in support of our view'
claims.note: D&S cite Cooper & Washburn as 1949 (Trans. Am. Fish. Soc., the 1946 volume printed in 1949), not 1946. They suggest the caged fish's capture, handling and sudden exposure lowered their resistance

tried.note: FAO catalogue page with excerpts; no PDF link

notes: Also in Table 1 p. 44: largemouth 4–14 g, 25–35 °C, estimated 24-h tolerance limits 0.9–1.4 mg/L at constant O₂ and 0.8–1.2 under gradually declining O₂ (Moss & Scott 1961). p. 71: Burdick, Dean & Harris 1957 measured yellow perch at about 12–21 °C. The review's general point (p. 54, PDF p. 65): Moore's caged-fish values are 'misleading', and laboratory endurance limits can differ from tolerance thresholds under natural conditions.
